prompt: What three parts does the lesson give a prescriptive question?
hint: None of them is a forecast.

choices.text: A forecast, a range and a horizon
choices.why: Those are the parts of a forecast, lesson 8. A prescriptive question uses a forecast as an input.

choices.text: Options, constraints and an objective
choices.why: Right: what could be done, what limits it, and what it is for.

choices.text: Data, a model and a dashboard to show the answer
choices.why: Those are tools; the three parts are about the decision itself.

choices.text: A question, a cause and an honest sentence
choices.why: That is the shape of a diagnosis, lesson 7.

prompt: Match each fact about the hose reel to the part of the prescriptive question it belongs to.
hint: Options, constraints, objective, and the forecast that feeds them.

pairs.left: Order now, or wait a week
The supplier sells in boxes of 30
Never run out, with as little stock as possible
The warehouse ships 18 reels a day

prompt: Why does the lesson say an analyst should not settle the objective silently inside a formula?
hint: "Never run out" against "as little stock as possible".

choices.text: Because a formula cannot hold an objective at all
choices.why: It can, which is the danger: the choice ends up buried in a cell.

choices.text: Because objectives belong in the documentation, not in the sheet
choices.why: Where it is written matters less than who chose it.

choices.text: Weighing goals that pull apart is a business decision, not the analyst's
choices.why: Right: two people with the same forecast and different objectives can both be right.

choices.text: Because the objective changes every month
choices.why: It may stay the same for years; the point is who owns it.

prompt: A team buys optimisation software to plan deliveries, and sets its objective to "fewest kilometres". Customers start receiving orders late. What went wrong, in the lesson's terms?
hint: The size does not change the shape.

choices.text: It found the best answer to the wrong objective
choices.why: Right: on-time delivery was never in the objective or the constraints, so the solver traded it away.

choices.text: The software was too simple for a problem of that size, and a stronger one is needed
choices.why: A stronger solver would find fewer kilometres faster, and the orders would be later still.

choices.text: The forecast of orders was wrong
choices.why: Nothing says the forecast was off; the routes did what the objective asked.

choices.text: Deliveries cannot be optimised by software
choices.why: They can, with the right objective and constraints.

prompt: A product sells 25 units a day, the supplier takes 6 days, and the safety stock is 3 days of demand. What is the reorder point, in units?
In your sheet, type 10 in B18 for the new lead time. What reorder point does B20 show?
Where did Caio's four safety days come from?

choices.text: From the highest day of demand, 22, minus the average of 18
choices.why: That difference is 4 by coincidence, and it is in reels, not days.

choices.text: From the latest delivery in the last year, four days late
choices.why: Right: the safety stock covers the worst lateness seen so far.

choices.text: From an industry standard for garden products
choices.why: The lesson cites no standard; the number comes from Varanda's own supplier.

choices.text: From the number of days it takes to unload a delivery at the warehouse in Contagem
choices.why: Unloading is not in the rule; lateness is.

prompt: The supplier now takes 10 days, and nobody changed the reorder point from 198. What happens when a delivery comes four days late?

choices.text: Nothing, because the safety stock covers four days of lateness
choices.why: It covered four days at a seven-day lead time. At ten days, three of those four are gone.

choices.text: The sales data shows a drop of 54 reels, and the next forecast corrects it
choices.why: The lost sales leave no receipt, so a forecast built on sales would learn the wrong lesson.

choices.text: The shelf is empty for three days, and no receipt records the loss
choices.why: Right: 11 days of cover against 14 needed, and a sale that never happens leaves no trace.

choices.text: The rule raises the order on its own
choices.why: The rule only knows the inputs it was given, and 7 was never changed.

prompt: The cushion a reorder rule adds for late deliveries and busy days is called the safety ___.
A sofa sells for R$ 1,200 and costs R$ 700. What profit, in reais, do 50 of them earn, counting price minus cost?
Without a discount, a product earns R$ 40,000 a month. With a discount, it sells at R$ 1,100 and costs R$ 700. How many units must it sell to earn the same?
hint: Profit to match divided by the margin per unit.

prompt: 20% off sells 700 sets against 400, and earns less. Why?
hint: R$ 400 a set, before the discount.

choices.text: Because the extra sets were sold at a loss
choices.why: At R$ 800 each still earns R$ 200 over its cost of R$ 600.

choices.text: Because a promotion raises the store's other costs in December
choices.why: The lesson's profit counts only price minus cost; the gap comes from the margin alone.

choices.text: Each set's margin halves; 300 more sets do not make it up
choices.why: Right: R$ 200 × 700 is 140 thousand, against R$ 400 × 400, 160 thousand.

choices.text: Because sales were counted in thousands and profit in units
choices.why: Both columns are in thousands of reais.

prompt: What did Lívia recommend to Helena about the December promotion?
hint: The person who owns the objective chooses.

choices.text: 20% off, because it sells the most sets of the three
choices.why: That answers one objective and hides the R$ 20 thousand it costs in profit.

choices.text: No discount, because it earns the most profit
choices.why: It does, narrowly, but the gap to 10% is within the error of the estimate.

choices.text: No single option: the consequences of each
choices.why: Right: the analyst lays out the trade-off; Renata and Helena own the objective.

choices.text: To run all three options in different stores and compare
choices.why: An experiment is a reasonable idea, but it is not what she wrote.

prompt: Which of these are true of the three December options, on the team's estimates? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: 20% off needs 800 sets to match no discount's profit
choices.why: Right: 160 thousand divided by R$ 200 a set.

choices.text: 10% off is 13 sets short of matching it
choices.why: Right: 533 needed against 520 estimated.

choices.text: 10% off earns more than no discount
choices.why: On the estimates it earns 156 against 160; it would need 540 sets to pull ahead.

choices.text: Each option's sales rise by the same percentage as its discount
choices.why: 20% off raises sales by 40%, and 10% off by 17%.

prompt: Order these decisions from the best suited to automate to the least.
hint: Frequency, cost of a mistake, and whether it can be undone.
items: Reordering hose reels at the warehouse
Marking down plants that are about to wilt, each evening
Choosing the discount for December's garden set
trap: The markdown happens every evening like the reorder, but a wrong price is seen by customers at once, so it sits just after it.

prompt: The reorder rule raises draft orders that a person approves. What does the lesson say makes that approval worth anything?
hint: What does the approval screen show?

choices.text: That the person approves within an hour of the draft appearing
choices.why: Speed of approval without the reasons is the click the lesson warns about.

choices.text: That the screen shows the demand and lead time behind the order
choices.why: Right: a person who cannot see why the system proposed an order learns to approve without reading.

choices.text: That a director approves instead of the warehouse
choices.why: Seniority does not help if the reasons are hidden.

choices.text: That orders above a set limit are blocked until somebody checks them
choices.why: Flagging unusual orders helps, but only if the person can see why they are unusual.

prompt: Where does the lesson place a decision to close a store, and why?
hint: The three rows of the table.

choices.text: Automated, because the analysis can be made very precise
choices.why: Precision does not change how rare, costly and permanent the decision is.

choices.text: In the middle, with a person approving a draft from the system
choices.why: That suits frequent decisions; a store closes once.

choices.text: Wherever the CEO prefers, since it is her company
choices.why: She decides it, but the lesson's reasons are about the decision, not about her.

choices.text: Recommended to a person: it is rare, costly and cannot be undone
choices.why: Right: it sits on the right of every row of the table.

prompt: Automating a decision moves the ___ for it; it does not remove it, and somebody still has to own each input of the rule.
hint: "The system ordered it" is not an answer.

prompt: A lamp sells 12 a day, the supplier takes 5 days, and the safety stock is 2 days. What is the reorder point, in lamps?
Helena is offered a system that ranks the stores by profit every month and closes the lowest automatically. What does the lesson say about it?
hint: Frequency, cost, and whether it can be undone.

choices.text: It is fine if the ranking uses profit per square metre instead of total profit
choices.why: A better measure does not make an irreversible decision safe to automate.

choices.text: It should not be automated: it is rare, costly and cannot be undone
choices.why: Right: the ranking can feed a recommendation, with its assumptions written out, and a person decides.

choices.text: It is fine with a person approving each closure with a click
choices.why: A click on a decision this size is the approval without reading that the lesson warns about.

choices.text: It is fine once it has been backtested on the last two years
choices.why: A backtest checks a forecast; it does not change what a closure costs if it is wrong.

prompt: Which inputs of the reorder rule need an owner who notices when they change? Choose all that apply.
hint: The rule shows what it was computed from.

choices.text: The supplier's lead time
choices.why: Right: 7 became 10, and the rule did not know.

choices.text: The average daily demand
choices.why: Right: demand moves with the season and with the product's life.

choices.text: The safety days
choices.why: Right: they came from the worst lateness, which can get worse.

choices.text: The cell where the formula is typed
choices.why: Where it is typed changes nothing about the answer; the inputs do.
